The patient is a 36-year-old white
woman with a 5-year history of type
1 diabetes (diagnosed in 1992) and
hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto’s
thyroiditis (antimicrosomal antibodies
were positive at 1 : 40). After devel-
oping diabetes she experienced re-
peated episodes of ketoacidosis and

developed severe insulin resistance.
Insulin resistance was ameliorated
with insulin lispro (Humalog) via an
insulin pump; however, the mecha-
nism of insulin resistance and re-
sponse to insulin lispro, was not de-
termined. Approximately 2 years after
the diagnosis of diabetes (during the
summer of 1994) she started to de-
velop intermittent pain and stiffness
in her abdominal musculature. She
had an extensive negative workup for
her abdominal pain including liver
function studies, fecal fat studies, an
abdominal ultrasound, abdominal
computed tomography, and an endo-
scopic retrograde cholangiopancrea-
tography. By the autumn of 1994 she
had developed lower extremity weak-
ness with intermittent pain. Results of
the neurological examination was un-
remarkable except for decreased mus-
cle strength (3–4/5) in her left lower
extremity. Magnetic resonance imag-
ing of the brain and cervical spine
was normal. A sural nerve biopsy re-
vealed mild axonopathy, and a muscle
biopsy specimen showed mild dener-
vation and reinnervation. At the end
of 1995, in addition to her progres-
sive abdominal pain and lower ex-
tremity weakness, she developed in-
tense pain in her upper and lower ex-
tremities. The severity of the pain ne-
cessitated hospitalization for intra-
venous narcotics, which were ineffec-
tive. She also complained of rigidity
and spasms of her proximal muscles
making ambulation difficult. SMS
was diagnosed in 1996 by finding
high titers (> 1 : 1000) of GAD65 
autoantibodies in both the serum and
the CSF. The di
agnosis of SMS was
confirmed clinically by the improve-
ment in muscular pain and stiffness
with oral diazepam. An EMG per-

formed only after the initiation of di-
azepam and baclofen in February
1996 was read as normal, and two
subsequent EMGs performed in Oc-
tober 1996 and July 1997 during
continued treatment were also read
as normal. Initial treatment was a
combination of diazepam, baclofen,
and prednisone. Due to continued
pain and stiffness she began plasma-
pheresis and additional immunomod-
ulatory treatment with MMF, IVIG,
and cyclophosphamide. The patient
was homozygous for HLA DR3 and
DQ2. Islet cell antibodies (ICA)
were positive. ICA512 (IA2) and in-
sulin receptor antibodies were nega-
tive.
Her family history was significant
for type 1 diabetes, hypothyroidism,
breast cancer, and possible SMS.
One sister, who also had type 1 dia-
betes, died of breast cancer at the
age of 33 years. She had episodes of
muscular pain and stiffness but was
never evaluated for nor given the di-
agnosis of SMS. Her father and an-
other sister had a history of hypothy-
roidism. The sister was homozygous
for HLA DR3 and DQ2 and was
GAD65 autoantibody positive.
Our patient has been treated for
more than 2 years (Fig. 1 A). Initial
treatment beginning in February
1996 was a combination of diazepam
and baeclofen. Prednisone had already
been started at 10 mg/day in July
1994 to treat a severe insulin resis-
tance. Due to a limited response to
high-dose diazepam (240 mg/day)
plasmapheresis began in March 1996
and was performed three times per
week, MMF was given at 2 g/day,
and prednisone was increased to 60
mg/day in addition to diazepam and
baclofen. The data in Fig. 2 A
demonstrate the decrease in GAD65
autoantibody levels during plasma-
pheresis (3/weeks), prednisone, and
MMF treatment in March and April
1996. The GAD65 autoantibody in-
dex (which represents the relative
level of GAD65 autoantibodies) in
the plasma was above 1.0 before
plasmapheresis and decreased to 0.4
after first plasmapheresis treatment
and remained at a lower level with
continued treatment (Fig. 2 A). The
intensive plasmapheresis and im-
munosuppressive therapy signifi-
cantly improved the clinical symp-
toms of SMS and allowed her to
gradually decrease the diazepam
dose from 240 mg/day to 40–80
mg/day in 2 months. During this pe-
riod she continued baclofen 60
mg/day. GAD65 autoantibody levels
during plasmapheresis (2/weeks),
prednisone, and MMF treatment in
May and June 1996 are shown in
Fig. 2 B. Due to her increased mobil-
ity, plasmapheresis was reduced to
twice per week and prednisone ta-
pered to 10 mg/day by May 1996.
Neurological examination revealed
normal sensation; roughly normal
muscle strength throughout; deep
tendon reflexes (DTR) were normal
except 1+ in her lower extremities
bilaterally.
In order to further decrease
GAD65 autoantibody levels as well
as the frequency of plasmapheresis
to improve quality of life, she re-
ceived IVIG at the dose of 0.5 g/kg
once per week while continuing
other therapies in late June 1996.
The GAD65 autoantibodies were
successfully maintained at low levels
during plasmapheresis (2/weeks),
prednisone, MMF, and IVIG treat-
ment in July and August 1996 
(Fig. 2 C). Comparing the GAD65
autoantibody level before and during
IVIG treatment showed that IVIG
had no effect on reducing the
GAD65 autoantibody level (GAD65
autoantibody index before was 
0.377 ± 0.038 compared to 0.376 ±
0.048 during IVIG, P > 0.05). Al-
though IVIG caused slight nausea
and vomiting, her stiffness decreased
and mobility improved. During this
period she did not experience muscu-

1+ in her lower extremities bilater-
ally.
By the end of August 1996, at a
diazepam dose of 10 mg/day, muscu-
lar stiffness and leg weakness re-
curred. MMF was discontinued and a
trial of cyclophosphamide began in
September 1996 (Fig. 2 D). Follow-
ing a protocol similar to that for
treating systemic lupus erythemato-
sus with plasmaphereis, she received
an intravenous infusion of 1700 mg
cyclophosphamide after three con-
secutive plasmaphereses on 11 Sep-
tember 1996. Plasmapheresis was
then stopped for 3 weeks. Due to the
development of neutropenia, oral cy-
clophosphamide (50 mg/day) was
not begun until 27 September 1996.
She was then treated with oral cy-
clophosphamide for 2 weeks. During
cyclophosphamide treatment she
continued to take prednisone (10 mg/
day) and high-dose baclofen (300 mg/
day) without diazepam, but the
GAD65 autoantibody level returned
to the level present prior to plasma-
pheresis treatment (Fig. 2 D). Restart-
ing plasmapheresis (2/weeks) again
gradually decreased GAD65 autoan-
tibody levels. She complained of
markedly increased stiffness, muscle
spasms, and weakness in her legs,
which significantly decreased her
mobility. Neurological examination
revealed normal sensation; muscle
strength 4/5 throughout; deep tendon
reflexes were 1+ in her biceps patella
jerk on the right.
Plasmapheresis (2/weeks) with
IVIG was therefore restarted in early
October 1996. Stiffness gradually de-
creased and mobility increased by No-
vember 1996. Neurological examina-
tion revealed normal sensation; mus-
cle strength 5/5 throughout; deep ten-
don reflexes were 2–3+ and symmet-
rical throughout. However, IVIG
started to cause severe nausea and
vomiting, and therefore it was discon-
tinued in the middle of November
1996. Plasmapheresis was continued
twice per week through February
1997, maintaining GAD65 autoanti-
bodies at lower levels (Fig. 2 E). The
plasmapheresis was then decreased to
once per week, which has continued
through the present time. The levels
of GAD65 autoantibodies in May 1997
are shown in Fig. 2 F. The patient de-
veloped a Staphylococcus aureus line
infection with endocarditis in May
1997. She was hospitalized, treated
with vancomycin, and stopped plasma-
pheresis for 2 weeks. Once again, the
GAD65 autoantibody level rose to the
level prior to plasmapheresis treat-
ment. Restarting plasmapheresis again
reduced the GAD65 autoantibody
level. As the plasmapheresis decreased
in frequency and amount, baclofen
was once again increased (360 mg/
day), resulting in severe nausea and
vomiting. Therefore in August 1997
she received intrathecal baclophen via
a pump resulting in resolution of nau-
sea and vomiting. The patient contin-
ued to receive plasmapheresis
(1/week), intrathecal baclofen and di-
azepam 5 mg/day with stabilization of
stiffness and muscular pain.
Plasmapheresis in our patient sig-
nificantly reduced GAD65 autoanti-
body levels and was associated with
marked clinical improvement.
Plasmapheresis over 28 months has
continued to maintain lower plasma
levels of GAD65 autoantibodies and
controlled clinical symptoms of
SMS; temporarily stopping plasma-
pheresis resulted in the rebound of
GAD65 autoantibody levels and sig-
nificantly increased stiffness and
spasms. Restoring treatment caused
symptom regression.
The clinical benefit of plasma-
pheresis for the treatment of SMS
has produced inconsistent results.
The beneficial effect of plasmaphere-
sis in a patient with SMS was first

described by Vicari et al. [17] and
has since been reported by others
[15, 18, 19]. Plasmapheresis not only
resulted in clinical and electromyo-
graphic improvement but also re-
duced GAD autoantibody titer. In con-
trast, Harding et al. [16] reported that
plasmapheresis in combination with
immunosuppression had no benefi-
cial effect in their SMS patients.
Plasmapheresis has also been
used to treat type 1 diabetes. Plasma-
phereis transitionally decreased the
islet cell antibody titer and improved
C-peptide and HbA
1c levels [25–29].
In this study our patient’s diabetic
condition remained unchanged
throughout all treatments including
high-dose prednisone. During the in-
tensive plasmapheresis and immuno-
therapy period her diabetic condition
and insulin resistance was improved
as demonstrated by decreased HbA
lc
and lispro insulin doses. This may
have been associated with the benefi-
cial effect of plasmapheresis, the
other immunosuppressive therapies,
or both.
Successful treatment with IVIG
has been reported in a number of dis-
orders, including myasthenia gravis,
multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré
syndrome, demyelinating polyneu-
ropathy, and polymyositis [30]. Sev-
eral case reports have also shown a
beneficial effect in the treatment of
SMS [20, 21, 24]. Our patient re-
ceived IVIG treatment once per
week for 3 months in addition to
plasmapheresis and prednisone. Dur-
ing the IVIG treatment period the pa-
tient felt significant clinical improve-
ment of SMS, although IVIG treat-
ment did not seem to reduce the
serum GAD65 autoantibody level.
The clinical benefit with the use of
IVIG in our patient is consistent with
that reported by other studies.
Other immunosuppressive thera-
pies have also been utilized in the
treatment of SMS [22, 23]. Our pa-
tient had additionally been treated
with a combination of prednisone,
MMF, and plasmapheresis, with clin-
ical improvement continually associ-
ated with declining GAD65 antibody
levels. Most of our patient’s clinical
improvement was probably sec-
ondary to plasmapheresis, as little in-
fluence on GAD65 autoantibody lev-
els was seen with MMF or cy-
clophosphamide administration.
In summary, we found that plasma-
pheresis was effective in controlling
clinical symptoms of SMS and re-
ducing the GAD65 autoantibody
level in our patient. Other adjunctive
immunotherapies may have some
clinical benefits but did not alter the
GAD65 autoantibody level in the
serum.
